title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day
titleZh: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day
author: cdrnsf
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The LatestUS technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.South Korea’s Kospi index lost 5.5% at end of trading. Photograph: Yonhap/EPAChris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

comments.author: seiferteric
comments.textRawHtml: I am trying to understand something about the economy and AI. If AI disrupts an industry that previously had high wages and now can be automated by commodity AI products, would it not actually lower GDP in some way (initially anyway)? What I mean is, if you had an industry that was worth say $1 billion, but now that same industry could be automated and done cheaply then it is no longe worth $1 billion? In some ways this is beneficial to the economy in that has reduced the cost of this industry and so customers see a benefit of cheaper products, but how would it benefit say AI companies since they are not capturing a $1 billion industry, but instead sort of destroying a $1 billion industry? I am mainly looking at this from the perspective of the value of an AI company.. If they just keep commoditizing industries and there is ample competition between AI companies, then how is the AI company capturing value such that they would be worth as much money as people are saying they are worth (trillions of dollars)? I know that there is more to this, like freeing up this money and labor could lead to new industries etc., but how much of this will actually go to AI companies?

children.author: FunkyMushroom
children.textRawHtml:
The related economic concept here is the Broken Window Fallacy. Doing 'redundant' work doesn't improve the economy, because there's an opportunity cost doing to anything. And replacing the need to "fix broken windows" or do now-AI-automated work would free up that opportunity cost. Which is how it's worked for nearly all automation. (Though Computers are subject to long running debate about this. See the Solow Productivity Paradox)

The gigawatt-sized asterisk on all of this is that AI companies have to capture that $1 billion. Anthropic has to ten-fold increase it's revenues or it goes bankrupt under it's current commitments. It has to increase it's revenues another 10 times to reach the $10,000,000,000,000/yr revenue required to support it's current valuation.

Anthropic put their Total Addressable Market at 35% of Global GDP (~$40 trillion/yr). They're planning to capture all of the money.

The second gigawatt-sized asterisk is that because of the fine handiwork of Mr. Huang, China has made very competitive AI models available for free, so the actual ability for AI companies to capture the value of the labour they displace ends up being quite limited. Thus a problem in the predictions: Something as to break, but it is as of yet unclear what that will be. Maybe Chinese AI will be banned, maybe Anthropic & OpenAI go bankrupt.

children.author: cogman10
children.textRawHtml:
The big issue with all this is that people whose jobs are destroyed by automation very rarely end up seeing improvements to their standard of living. And with the modern system, people are pretty boned if they chose the wrong career.

The luddite movement is informative here. When manufactures found ways to mass produce goods eliminating jobs left and right, the people in the skilled trades whose jobs were eliminated did not benefit in the slightest from the economic progress.

We now live in an era of diminishing jobs which provide livable wages. It's why so many economies have moved to require everyone to participate in the labor market just to achieve the basics.

Put more simply, broken windows harm society as a whole, but they do make glazers and the people who support the glazers happy. Now that we live in an era where a significant portion of the population is glazers so-to-speak and ai threatens to eliminate those jobs, it looks like the only path forward for those glazers is low wage jobs.

children.author: jvanderbot
children.textRawHtml:
I got coffee with a nice person from HN today. They were wearing a hat with the word "Luddite" on it. I knew what it meant but asked anyway - yes it's not anti-tech, it's anti automation and loss of craft.

The thing about luddites is that yes they wanted to preserve human craftsmanship, and as you say it didn't work. John Henry died. Luddites worked in factories and declined into poverty. Hopeless. Doomed.

But, I am cranking down my personal backlog with AI tools, using them at work, and loving the usefulness of them. It doesn't feel like I'm a master weaver who has their work automated, it feels like I'm reaping productivity gains.

Was there ever a moment in the Luddite movement when some of them leaned in and had fun? Did some of John Henry's colleagues just really enjoy the new steam drivers?

It doesn't _feel_ like I'm being forced out of my trade. I sincerely doubt the Luddites had a moment where they happily shelled out the 1820 equivalent of $20/m to get access to a weaving machine. I'm not saying "this time is different", but I am saying everyone tells me to not use AI, and to be afraid, and I'm de-skilling or whatever, etc. How do we all _know_ what is right?

A loom does not bring agency. It takes it. But I feel like having a computer, access to LLM, increases my agency just a bit. It allows me to do more, not just do what I need to _faster_. It's not _just_ automation.

children.author: jvanderbot
children.textRawHtml:
The fundamental difference is that Looms were point process automation that cost capital. They took a job a person did and made it automatic so that the person could be fired in exchange for up front cost.

The weaver couldn't build the machine, maintain it, adapt it, take it home, use it for other processes, try their own creative designs, open a competing shop, work in other textiles etc.

But agentic tools are not that. They DO allow all that. In fact software engineering has always been about automating things, and agentic tools just allow more people to automate more things, AND create more software the way they want it.

LLMs just don't feel like a loom. They feel something that can be used by workers themselves. Like power tools. A very generic power tool. That's essentially free. Unlike all automation to date which required massive up front capital to automate one single process.

Maybe that's the difference - accessibility and generalization.

children.author: CamperBob2
children.textRawHtml:
I think the Luddites' beef was more about losing options, as they watched their sense of agency in their lives and careers slip away. They couldn't rent their own automated looms for the equivalent of $20/month. Those things were expensive, exotic machines usable only in industrial settings, more like NVL72 racks than RTX 5090s. But with AI, we are as you suggest gaining options, so any comparison with Luddism fails from the get-go.

Obviously the correct way to view the arrival of AI is as an empowering tool for the ultimate benefit of us all, but just as obviously there are a lot of people who simply don't seem capable of understanding that. Obviously the correct way to react to the arrival of AI is to severely regulate the monopolists and oligarchs rather than the technology itself, but... see above.

Unfortunately there is no obvious way to deal with people who think the Luddites were somehow morally superior, or who otherwise want to rehabilitate or emulate them. It's like flashing back to late 2019, watching news reports come in about some sort of weird, unusually-severe flu that seemed to be spreading. Nobody knew for sure what to do then, and I don't think anyone does now. But we are going to have to do something to keep those people from dragging us backward with the self-centered psychological pandemic they are trying to spread.
